meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You've made this day a special day, by just your being you'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Fred Rogers said it under oath in 1969, quoting his own sign-off. The on-air wording was slightly different. Here's the transcript.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1928–2003 · Presbyterian minister, host of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and unusually well documented for a Fred Rogers line. He spoke these exact words on 1 May 1969 before the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications, introducing them as how he ended every episode: the hearing was filmed, and Current’s transcription of the video reproduces the sentence verbatim.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Testimony before the U.S. Senate Subcommittee on Communications
Fred Rogers, questioned by Sen. John Pastore (D-R.I.)
The closing words of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, quoted by Rogers in the hearing

source.excerpt: I give an expression of care every day to each child, to help him realize that he is unique. I end the program by saying, “You’ve made this day a special day, by just your being you. There’s no person in the whole world like you, and I like you, just the way you are.”
trail: Wikiquote carries the sentence in its sourced Fred Rogers section ↗, cited to his testimony before a U.S. Senate committee on 1 May 1969.
The public-media trade journal Current publishes a transcription of the hearing ↗, marked “Transcription from video verified,” in which Rogers speaks the line word for word.
Footage of the appearance is hosted by the programme’s own site, Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood ↗.
Wikipedia’s account of the hearing ↗ confirms the setting: Senator John Pastore’s subcommittee, a proposed halving of a $20 million appropriation, and the full sum granted.
source.excerptNote: One caveat on dating: Wikipedia and Wikiquote both place the testimony on 1 May 1969, while Current’s archival reprint of the transcript is filed under 2 May 1969 and says the same in its introduction. The wording of the line is identical either way.

sourceLink.text: Read the full transcript at Current

source.rightsHolder: Fred Rogers Productions (the company founded as Family Communications, Inc.) and the Estate of Fred Rogers
source.rightsNote: These are Fred Rogers’s own words from 1969, and a witness’s testimony is not a work of the U.S. Government simply because it was given in a hearing room. The sentence is also the sign-off of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, produced from 1971 by Family Communications, Inc., now Fred Rogers Productions ↗. Treat it as in copyright and quote it with attribution rather than reproducing it commercially.

author.name: Fred Rogers
author.heading: Who was Fred Rogers?
author.metaLine: 1928–2003 · Presbyterian minister and creator of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood
author.bio: Fred McFeely Rogers was born in Latrobe, Pennsylvania on 20 March 1928 and ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1963 — with an unusual charge: to serve children through television. He hosted, wrote, scored and puppeteered Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood from 1968 to 2001, treating anger, divorce, death and self-worth as things a four-year-old deserved to hear discussed honestly. He died of stomach cancer in Pittsburgh on 27 February 2003.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — rare for a name this heavily counterfeited. What travels loose is the wording and the setting.

items.why: Viewers who remember the television closing usually remember a present-tense version. Wikipedia records the broadcast closing ↗ as “You always make each day a special day. You know how: By just your being you…” The famous past-tense form is the one Rogers used when quoting himself to the Senate.

The line is spoken, not sung. It does not appear in the lyrics of the closing song Rogers wrote — the Neighborhood Archive’s lyric page ↗, which dates the song to 1970, contains neither “special day” nor “just your being you.”

items.who: Fred Rogers as a quote magnet
items.why: Plenty of warm sayings pinned on Rogers belong to other people. Quote Investigator credits “There isn’t anyone you couldn’t love once you’ve heard their story” ↗ to Mary Lou Kownacki — Rogers shared it, and his wife Joanne said Kownacki deserved the credit. The three-fold “be kind” saying traces to Henry James ↗, and Rogers credited James himself.

misattribution.truthLine: This one is his. He said it into a microphone in a Senate hearing room on 1 May 1969, and the transcript verified against the video ↗ has him introducing it with four words: “I end the program by saying…”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Nixon administration wanted to halve public broadcasting’s $20 million appropriation. On 1 May 1969 a soft-spoken children’s presenter with a $6,000 programme budget sat down in front of Senator John Pastore’s communications subcommittee, declined to read his prepared statement, and simply described what he did.

Six minutes in, having quoted this sentence as the thing he says to every child at the end of every episode, he had turned the room. Pastore’s reply is on the record: he admitted to goosebumps, then told Rogers he had just earned the twenty million dollars.
detailsBody: His case was not sentimental. He contrasted his $6,000 half-hour with the cost of two minutes of animated “bombardment,” and argued that dramatising the inner life of childhood — haircuts, sibling anger, ordinary family friction — was better television than gunfire.
The line about being special was the proof of concept: an expression of care delivered daily, by name, to a child who might not hear one anywhere else that day.
context.pull: A grown man reciting a child’s song to other grown men — and it worked.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section gives the wording "You've made this day a special day, by just your being you. There's no person in the whole world like you; and I like you just the way you are." cited to testimony before a U.S. Senate committee, May 1, 1969.

Current's transcription of the hearing, marked "Transcription from video verified," reproduces Rogers saying "I end the program by saying, 'You've made this day a special day, by just your being you. There's no person in the whole world like you, and I like you, just the way you are.'" It also names Sen. John Pastore, the Senate Commerce Committee's communications subcommittee, and the $20 million appropriation, and dates the testimony 2 May 1969.

Wikipedia dates the testimony to May 1, 1969, before the Senate Subcommittee on Communications chaired by John Pastore, over a proposed cut from $20 million to $10 million, with the full $20 million ultimately granted.
The official Mister Rogers' Neighborhood site hosts video titled "Fred Rogers testifies before the Senate Subcommittee on Communications 1969."

Wikipedia records the on-air spoken closing as "You always make each day a special day. You know how: By just your being you/yourself. There's only one person in the whole world that's like you..." and lists the show's production companies as Small World Enterprises (1968-1971) and Family Communications (1971-2001).
The Neighborhood Archive page for "It's Such a Good Feeling" states Fred Rogers wrote the song in 1970, and its printed lyrics contain neither "special day" nor "just your being you."

Quote Investigator concludes Mary Lou Kownacki deserves credit for "There isn't anyone you couldn't love once you've heard their story," a saying sometimes attributed directly to Fred Rogers; his wife Joanne stated Kownacki deserved the credit.
Quote Investigator traces the threefold "be kind" saying to Henry James, and notes Fred Rogers used it while crediting James.
Quote Investigator's Fred Rogers category page lists investigations into sayings credited to him; it contains no article on "You've made this day a special day" or "just your being you."

Wikipedia gives Fred McFeely Rogers's dates as born March 20, 1928 in Latrobe, Pennsylvania, died February 27, 2003 in Pittsburgh of stomach cancer; ordained a Presbyterian minister in 1963; Mister Rogers' Neighborhood ran 1968-2001.
Family Communications, Inc. was formed in 1971, became The Fred Rogers Company in 2010 and Fred Rogers Productions in 2018, and produced Mister Rogers' Neighborhood.
